div.head: Controller Area Network ( C A N ) is widely used in real-time automobile control and is gaining wider acceptance as a standard for factory automation. This paper discusses the applicability of Earliest Deadline (EDF) techniques to the scheduling of CAN messages. Earliest deadline can guarantee higher network utilization than jked-priority schemes like Deadline or
div.p: Rate Monotonic (DM, RM), but it is dificult to implement in local area networks or local buses. The reason is the need f o r updating the deadlines (priorities) at each scheduling round and the limited numer of priority levels offered by the arbitration protocol. This deadline encoding problem results in an additional priority inversion factor when considering the schedulability analysis of hard real-time messages. This paper describes an effective deadline encoding method and discusses its implementation and its effects o n the guarantee analysis. In spite of a limited processor overhead (less than 5% of CPU time) the proposed EDF implementation allows a increase (up to 20%) in the feasible network workload. This trade off will be made more convenient as controller technology evolves.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The CAN (Controller Area Network) bus (standard ISO/DIS 11898) is a broadcast digital bus designed to operate at speeds from 20kb/s to 1Mb/s. The protocol, originally developed by Bosch [3, 4, 51, has become a standard defacto for automotive control. The CAN is an attractive solution for embedded control systems because of its low cost, light protocol man- agement and the deterministic resolution of the contention.

Its major limitation is in the maximum available bandwidth, which is a consequence of adopting a multi-master digital bus. The CAN protocol works using a collision detection and resolution scheme. The message to be transmitted among all competing messages at the nodes is chosen according to its identifier. The lowest (highest) identifier message is transmitted. This makes possible to encode the message priority into the identifier field and to implement priority-based real-time scheduling of periodic and aperiodic messages. Early results on scheduling the CAN bus have been described in [14] and [15], where a schedulability analysis of real-time message streams having a fixed priority (possibly assigned by Rate-Monotonic or Deadline-Monotonic schemes, originally developed in [9] and [7]) is presented.

Static priority scheduling protocols (like Rate Monotonic or RM and Deadline Monotonic or DM) have many advantages, the most significant in this case being an extremely simple implementation and good efficiency in the exploitation of the available channel bandwidth. CAN allows a number of priority levels that is more than necessary to encode the priorities of the messages as required by RM or DM.

However, while it can be a simple and effective solution, static priority scheduling might not always be the best one. Zuberi and Shin [16] [17] have shown how dynamic scheduling (Earliest Deadline or EDF) can prove significantly better than static scheduling (e.g. Deadline Monotonic or DM [7]) when scheduling realistic loads with a share of sporadic messages on controller area networks. Results in [17] show up to a 20% difference in network utilization. Our preliminary simulations, shown in figure 1 for task sets of 30 periodic tasks having periods ranging from 3ms to 2s, confirmed the figures.

Zuberi and Shin proposed a scheduling 0 , =. . method (MTS) which is a trade off between a static priority assignment (DM) and a dynamic one (EDF). This compromise was considered necessary in order to save the processor time necessary to the implementation of pure EDF.

The research focused on manifacturing applications with a mix of periodic and sporadic realtime messages and the authors proved how the increased network utilization allowed by a dynamic scheduling scheme (be MTS or EDF) can be a critical factor. Gaining a few percentage points of network utilization, in this case, might be worth spending a little fraction of processor time (which is expected to decrease considering the constant evolution in processor speed). This is especially true for controller area networks where the available bandwidth (the maximum allowed by the standard is 1 Mb/s) will always be limited by the laws of physics (the time it takes the signal to travel the bus).

The objective of this research is to study the conditions for implementing true earliest deadline scheduling in CAN networks. The first step is to find the (analytical) condition for scheduling real-time messages on controller area networks based on earliest deadline techniques. Later, we will discuss limitations and problems in the implementation of the method on the existing standard using current technologies (Infineon and Motorola controllers with integrated CAN devices).

The work focuses on a deadline encoding method that maps a possibly wide range of deadlines into a limited number of priority levels and minimizes the priority inversions. A natural way to compute the priorities of the messages from the deadline (relative or absolute) is to divide the temporal axis in equal size U- nits (MTS uses this form of linear encoding). An alternative approach assumes time quantization with intervals of exponentially increasing size. The practical applicability of the method is discussed and an algorithm for checking the schedulability of periodic and aperiodic messages is presented.

The algorithm is obtained by extending the reasoning in [16] and [lo]. The paper gives an evaluation of the overall penalty on the schedulability formula and an estimate on the expected processor overhead. The method will be evaluated with experimental runs. The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 contains a very short description of the CAN standard, Section 3 contains a discussion on the implementation of EDF on CAN networks; a method to efficiently map message deadlines into priorities and the schedulability analysis. Section 4 contains additional discussion on the implementation of the method and Section 5 ends the study with the presentation of the experimental results.

div.head: Controller Area Networks and Message Scheduling
div.p: The CAN bus consists of a single shared digital channel for distributed real-time control systems. The standard specification defines the physical and data-link layers, message routing and bus arbitration.

The bus is a wired OR (or wired AND) channel connecting all nodes. The media access protocol works by alternating contention and transmission phases. The time axis is divided in slots which must be larger than or equal to Tp = 2L/Vp, the time it takes the signal to travel back and forth along the channel, L is the length of the bus and V, is the propagation speed of the signal. The contention and transmission phases take place during the digital transmission of the frame bits. This limits the maximum available bit rate to the theoric bound B,,, = l/Tp (actually lower because of imprecise synchronization, local processing and safety margins) or conversely, it limits the channel length given the desired bit rate.

The CAN protocol has the message format of figure 2 where the size of the fields is expressed in bits. Priorities are encoded in the message identifier field (11 bits wide for the standard format, 29 for the extended format). The identifier is used not only for bus arbitration, but also describes the meaning of the data (the message stream). The standard requires that all contending messages have a unique i-dentifier (unique purity). This means that not all of the 11 bits in the identifier field can be used to encode the priority of the message (or its deadline). Nodes can set message filters to select only those identifiers they are interested in receiving. The other fields are: the control field containing information on the type of message, the data field, containing the actual data to be transmit- ted, the checksum, used to check the correctness of the message bits, the acknowledge (ACK), used to acknowledge the reception, the ending delimiter (ED) used to signal the end of the message and the idle space (IS) used to separate one frame from the following.

If a node wishing to transmit finds the channel idle, it waits for the next slot and starts an arbitration phase by issuing a start of frame bit. At this point each node having a message to send can contend for the channel transmitting the identifier (priority) bits of the message during the arbitration slots, one bit for each slot starting from the most significant.

Suppose the collisions among the identifier bits are solved with a logical AND. If a node reads its priority bits on the channel without any change, it realizes it is the winner of the contention and gets the rights to transmit. If one of its bits appears changed when read from the bus, this means there is an higher priority contending message and it withdraws. For example, figure 3 shows three contending nodes with the corresponding binary priorities and the result of the arbitration phase.

Consider working with the standard format: if n bits (out of 11) are used to encode the priority (deadline) of the message, ll -n are available to identify the message stream. If only one message from a given stream can be active at any instant, then each contending message will have a unique identifier.

div.head: Earliest Deadline Scheduling: Implementation Issues and the Deadline Encoding Problem
div.p: Earliest deadline scheduling (EDF) works by giving higher priority to the message having the earliest absolute deadline. EDF is the basis of many real-time processor scheduling algorithms because of its high utilization. Neverthless it is rarely used to schedule messages in real-time networks. The reasons have been explicitly stated in [16]:

Absolute deadlines become larger and larger as time progresses. Eventually they would require a very large number of bits for an efficient encoding. Relative deadlines with respect to the time instant when the arbitration round starts tSTART (alternatively, slack times) could be represented with much higher precision but require to be updated at each arbitration round.

Even if relative deadlines could be computed at each round, a typical communication workload in a manifacturing environment ( [16]) contains messages with a wide range of relative deadlines (from the fraction of millisecond to a few seconds). Mapping these deadlines in the small number of priority bits allowed by the existing protocols is not an easy task.

The last problem has been solved by Katcher where di is the absolute deadline of Mi and tsTART is the starting time of the contention (computed every time a contention starts). This assignment corresponds to the Earliest Deadline First policy. The mapping of a possibly very large range of relative deadlines di -TART into the limited number of priority bits allowed by the protocol is probably the major problem that we face when scheduling messages with earliest deadline techniques.

Both [6] and [16] contain hints on the possible use of a logarithmic quantization of the deadlines (periods in [6] since the theory applies to Rate Monotonic), but this solution was rejected in [16] because of the need for updating the deadlines at each contention and in spite of its best performance when scheduling the messages in the experimental sets. In (161 the authors proposed to divide the message set in high-speed and low-speed messages, the first to be scheduled using MTS, a method implementing an approximation of EDF over time epochs (dividing the deadline range in equal-size slots) and the latter by deadline monotonic (DM).
The effects of deadline quantization can easily be explained by example. Consider what happens to messages MI and M2 of figure 4.

In our case (figure 4) deadlines d2 and dl belong to the same section Ik, therefore MI and M2 have identical priority k and nothing prevents M2 from being scheduled before MI. This event can be considered a priority inversion (the lower priority message gets scheduled first) when scheduling messages with EDF.

To reduce the cost of priority inversions it is possible to map deadlines into priorities us- ing a logarithmic scale, that is, a scale in which the unit is not constant, but is exponentially increased. The temporal axis is divided in sections Ik of exponentially increasing length 6 k , which are all further divided in a constant number of units. In this way we have a finer resolution for nearer deadlines, and a coarser resolution for further deadlines. The proposal was initially formulated in [6] and later reappeared in [l6], yet no analytical nor experimental study has ever been presented for EDF scheduling.

div.head: Computing the Relative Deadline
div.p: In [16] the possibility of computing the relative deadlines at each arbitration round has been quickly dismissed since this would put too much burden on the local CPU. This is not always the case for controller area networks. The CAN standard has its maximum transmission rate at lMB/s (maximum bus length 40m), but rates from lOkb to 500 kb/s are quite common, especially in factory automation environments. The maximum rate is inversely proportional to the maximum bus length since the arbitration scheme requires that the wave front of the signal propagates to the most remote node and back before the bit is sampled. At 125 kb/s the bus requires (at most) one arbitration every 0.86 ms (if the size of the data packet is 8 bytes), quite close to the 1 ms rate proposed in [16] for updating the scheduling parameters for a not so realistic 10Mb/s CAN. A modern 16 bit microcontroller like the Siemens (Infineon) C167CR with an integrated CAN module can execute instructions in 80 ns (at 25MHz) with an interrupt response time of 40011s and a single-instruction context switch [12]. Suppose computing the new relative deadline and encoding it into the available priority bits takes 300 instructions (we'll check this assumption later), then the processor overhead is in the range of 25 ps every 0.86 ms, that is less than 3%! Similar values can be obtained by considering the 25MHz -32 bit Motorola MC68376 with the integrated Toucan CAN device [ll]. Of course this might not be sufficient for a 1M-B/s network (unless a faster microcontroller or processor is used), but the technological trends will improve the feasibility of this option, since the bandwidth of CAN networks will always be limited by the need for the signal to travel twice the maximum bus length before the bit is sampled, while microcontrollers can (and will in the next future) exceed the 25MHz rate.

div.head: Experimental results
div.p: In order to assess the feasibility and the possible benefits deriving from a logarithmic encoding of deadlines a number of simulations have been performed. All simulations and experiments have been run considering a 250KHz CAN. The packet size has been assumed as fized (8 bytes). The network utilization appearing on the x axis in all graphs is the actual (data) utilization, that is ci ei/Ti (the resulting network utilization is higher because of protocol overheads). Full network utilization is achieved at approximately 0.58 of data utilization. The simulations (figure 8) have been performed on 36000 message sets (1000 message sets for each point in the graph) consisting of 30 periodic and sporadic message streams having periods (minimum interarrival times) between 3ms and 4s and deadline to period ratios in the range 0.8 to 1. The percentage of sporadic tasks is approximately 20%. 5 of the 11 identifier bits have been used to identify the 30 real-time message streams. The 6 remaining bits are used to encode 64 possible priority levels. The 64 levels have been used to define 8 time sections containing 8 units each. The number of nodes connected to the network (and generating the message streams) is 8. The graph in figure 8 plots the percentage of schedulable sets against the data utilization of the network and shows the possible advantages of earliest deadline scheduling and the effectiveness of logarithmic encoding of deadlines when compared to deadline monotonic scheduling. The continuous line shows the percentage of sets found schedulable when using DM; the dashed line shows the percentage of schedulable set when an idealized version of EDF was used, that is the contention was always won by the lowest deadline message (regardless of the actual number of available priority bits); finally, the dotted line shows the percentage of sets found schedulable when encoding the deadlines into the 64 priority levels using logarithmic quantization. The experimental data are in accordance with the results presented in [16].

Please note, for Xi eJTi x 0.35 the percentage of sets found schedulable by EDF or its approximation by logarithmic quantization is twice the percentage of sets scheduled by DM. Alternatively, if a given percentage of schedulable sets is considered, the data utilization is enhanced by almost 0.1 in the range 0.25-0.45, which is a sensible improvement over schedulability with DM. there was almost no difference between the simulation data obtained by using idealized ED-F and the data obtained by using logarithmic encoding of deadlines.

The second phase consisted in replicating the experiments by considering the results of the guaranteeability analysis instead of the results of simulation. Each point of the guarantee analysis graphs has been obtained by considering the result of 5000 runs. Each run consisted in the schedulability analysis of a message set composed by high rate messages, with periods from 3ms to 12ms and low rate messages with periods between 250ms and 1s. The percentage of guaranteeable sets (figure 9) is lower in all cases when compared to the percentage of the sets found schedulable in the simulations. The percentage of guaranteed sets when using logarithmic quantization is always within 2% of the percentage of sets guaranteed by EDF and much higher than the percentage of sets found schedulable by DM.

div.head: Comparing logarithmic EDF with MTS
div.p: Finally, a comparison between the implementation of EDF by logarithmic quantization and MTS was tried. Clearly, the performance of MTS relative to logarithmic EDF is workload dependent. A fair comparison would require the availability of real-world test cases, but the implementation details of most car controllers (for example) are not made available by manufacturers. The two methods have been compared by choosing sets of message streams modeled on the avionic task workload cited in [8]. This is the same approach taken in [17] where it is shown how MTS performs in between an ideal implementation of EDF and DM. In the first example (figure lo), the two algorithms have been compared when scheduling 60000 message sets (5000 message sets for each point in the graph) consisting of 3 sets of periodic and sporadic message streams having periods (minimum interarrival times) in the range (3ms, 12ms), (30ms, 267

In the second example (figure lo), the message sets consisted of 2 groups of periodic and sporadic message streams having periods (minimum interarrival times) in the range (3ms, 90ms), and (looms, 1s) respectively. The two algorithms performed almost identically until the data utilization was x 0.35, when the performance gap became larger and larger until it reached approximately 0.05% in data utilization and as much as 75% in the number of schedulable sets (data utilization M 0.45).

div.head: . Conclusions
div.p: A possible implementation of earliest deadline scheduling for real-time messages on Controller Area Networks has been shown. The paper shows a possible solution to the deadline encoding problem and contains a procedure to guarantee the deadlines of real-time messages in advance. The effectiveness of earliest deadline (dynamic) scheduling and its approximation, obtained by encoding relative deadlines with a logarithmic scale, has been proven by simulation. The results show that the percentage of guaranteed (or schedulable) messages can be much higher than the percentage of messages guaranteed by static priority encoding (deadline monotonic). The feasibility of the proposed solution has also been discussed with respect to the processor overhead that is necessary to implement the dynamic encoding of message priorities at each contention round.
